title: Agentic AI & Hyperautomation
meta_description: Agentic AI & Hyperautomation services from Dataq Software: scope, delivery pattern, platforms and committed outcomes.

blocks.x: Hyperautomation succeeds as workforce design, not as tool rollout. Agentic AI & Hyperautomation runs seven practices that mine the work, prove the ROI before the build, deploy role-scoped agents under policy bounds, and manage the resulting digital workforce with the same discipline — capacity, shifts, versioning, retirement — you apply to people.

Hyperautomation fails as a program when it is run as a tool rollout. It succeeds when it is run like workforce design: mine the work, prove the ROI, build small governed agents with real identity, and keep human checkpoints exactly where the risk register says they must be.

This domain runs that discipline across seven practices — from process mining through document intelligence to full digital-workforce orchestration. The shared substrate is the policy engine, the replay store and the ROI ledger; every practice contributes to and is constrained by them.

blocks.x: Why automation programs stall — and what the discipline is instead

Hyperautomation fails as a program when it is run as a tool rollout: licenses bought, bots deployed, nobody owning the coverage number. It succeeds when it is run like workforce design — mine the work with event-log evidence, prove the ROI before the build, deploy role-scoped agents under policy bounds, and manage the resulting digital workforce with capacity, versioning and retirement discipline.

The governance argument is what wins the board: every agent action replays, checkpoints sit where the risk matrix says they must, and autonomy is earned by evidence rather than configured by enthusiasm. That discipline is the difference between a program the auditors sign off and one they suspend.
The domain reference architecture — mined work to governed execution

One loop spans the domain: event-log mining feeds a conformance-checked candidate pipeline, funded candidates become policy-bounded agents, the orchestration layer carries durable state, and the fleet layer runs the resulting workforce. Checkpoints are placed by risk, and every action replays.

blocks.x: Candidate economics — where ideas die and why

The mining funnel is a kill pipeline by design: candidates die at conformance checks, at ROI screening, at checkpoint design — and the kill reasons are logged, because a defensible no is worth as much as a funded yes.

blocks.caption: Domain-level release gates — the evidence each demands
rows: Is the process real, or is it the org chart's fiction?
Event-log conformance metrics; variant coverage; owner sign-off
Policy conformance suite; least-privilege tool grants; deny-by-default evidence
Are human approvals placed by risk, not convenience?
Checkpoint map signed by the risk owner; bypass impossible by design
Does the workflow survive partial failure?
Chaos drills: kill agents mid-run, corrupt a message, revoke a token
Replay of sampled cases with full action traces and inputs
Is the automation paying for itself?
ROI ledger against the mined baseline, not a slide
